caption_hook: California has been an ocean trench, a granite mountain core and a volcano that blanketed the West in ash.

layers.name: BISHOP TUFF
layers.what: A huge eruption emptied a magma chamber and left the Long Valley near Mammoth. Glowing ash settled into a rock called tuff, hundreds of feet thick in places.
layers.bonus: Its ash fell as far away as Nebraska, and it is still found in Midwest soils.

layers.name: MONTEREY FORMATION
layers.what: Along the coast, a deep sea once filled with microscopic algae called diatoms. Their glassy shells sank, piled up and became this pale, thinly layered rock.
layers.bonus: It is the source rock for much of California's oil, and it folds like a stack of paper.

layers.name: SIERRA GRANITE
layers.what: Magma cooled slowly deep below an ancient volcanic arc and hardened into granite. Uplift and glaciers later stripped away the cover and exposed the Sierra Nevada.
layers.bonus: Half Dome and Mount Whitney, the tallest peak in the lower 48 at 14,505 ft, are both granite.

layers.name: FRANCISCAN COMPLEX
layers.hook: Ocean floor scraped off a trench
layers.what: Seafloor mud, sand and red chert were dragged into a subduction zone and scraped onto the continent. The result is a jumbled mix of rock types under the Bay Area.
layers.bonus: The Golden Gate Bridge's towers stand on this scrambled seafloor.

layers.name: LATHAM SHALE
layers.what: In the Cambrian, the Mojave region lay under a warm shallow sea. Mud buried trilobites and other early animals, and the shale now holds their fossils in the desert.
layers.bonus: Collectors split these rocks in the Marble Mountains to find trilobites over half a billion years old.

layers.name: BLACK MTNS GNEISS
layers.hook: The oldest rock in the valley
layers.what: Under Death Valley's mountains lies banded gneiss, rock baked and squeezed deep in the crust long before animals existed. Faulting later lifted it into view.
layers.bonus: Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America at 282 ft below sea level, sits at its foot.
